"La evaluación de desempeño" is the standard term for a performance review, and the two nouns are joined with "de". The article is compulsory for a subject noun.
"Salir bien" means "to turn out well". "Tan bien como" is the comparison of equality, and "más o menos" softens it — Spanish needs all three words for the effect English gets from "about as well as".
"Como salen siempre estas cosas" puts the verb before the subject, which Spanish does freely in subordinate clauses. "Siempre" sits between them without any awkwardness.
"Me dijeron" is a subjectless plural verb, the natural equivalent of the English passive "I was told". Spanish cannot make the person the subject of a passive here.
"Tener" plus a noun for a quality. The clause needs "que", which unlike English "that" can never be dropped. The quotation goes in angle quotes.
"Lo que" refers back to the whole quotation, and that is what the neuter "lo" signals. "Por lo visto" means "apparently", and "correos" is short for "correos electrónicos".
"Hubo" is the preterite of the impersonal "haber": it never agrees with what follows, so it is never "hubieron".
"Una sugerencia delicada" places the adjective after the noun. "Delicada" here means "gently put", not "fragile".
"De que" is compulsory after "sugerencia": the noun demands the preposition, and dropping it is a common mistake even among native speakers. "Podría" is the conditional, softening the whole thing.

"Nadie" before the verb takes no extra "no", but "nunca" after it is perfectly normal — Spanish allows the accumulation that English forbids. "Me ha explicado" uses the present perfect for experience up to now.
The indirect question keeps the written accent on "qué" even though there is no question mark.
"En la práctica" keeps the article, unlike English "in practice", which has none.
The preterite for a completed action. The written accent on "asentí" marks the stressed final syllable.
"Como se asiente" uses the impersonal "se" where English uses "you". "Asentir" is stem-changing: "asiento", "asientes", "asiente".
"Cuando" with the indicative, because this is a general truth rather than a future event. "Más larga" builds the comparative with "más".
"En conjunto" means "on balance, taken together".
"Yo diría" adds the pronoun for emphasis, which Spanish does only when it wants to. The conditional softens the verdict.
"Fueron cuarenta minutos" keeps the verb in the plural, agreeing with the minutes. The adjective follows the noun: "minutos productivos".
"Toparse con" is reflexive and takes "con". The preterite places it at a definite moment.
"La típica meseta" puts the adjective before the noun, which with "típico" adds a note of resignation. After it, "la meseta típica", it would sound merely descriptive.
"En el B1" keeps the article before the level name, which English does not. "Más o menos" softens the reference.
"Todo lo que" is a three-part frame using the neuter "lo". The verb "decía" is imperfect, for something that went on.
"Ser" for a lasting property, in the imperfect. "Técnicamente" means "strictly speaking" here.
The second adjective shares the same verb. "Inerte" is stronger and more literary than "sin vida".
"Lo que" opens a subject clause again. "Por fin" means "finally, at last".
"No fue un manual" negates the copula. This is the first half of the "no ... sino ..." frame.
"Sino" is the word for "but" after a negative and cannot be replaced by "pero". "De fútbol" links the nouns with "de".
"La mitad" keeps its article and takes a singular verb even when what follows is plural.
"Escapársele algo a alguien" is a three-part idiom: the thing escapes, "se" marks it as unintentional, and "me" says to whom. English says "went over my head", which is built quite differently.
"Resulta que" is an impersonal frame, "it turns out that". "Ahí estaba la clave" puts the verb before the subject, which Spanish does for emphasis.
"El ritmo del idioma" contracts "de" and "el" into "del". Both nouns keep their articles.
"Se coge" is the impersonal "se", "one picks up". "Mucho antes" uses "mucho" to intensify.
After a comparison comes "que". "El vocabulario" keeps the article, where English drops it.
"Sonar" is stem-changing: "sueno", "suenas", "suena". It is a linking verb here.
"Como una persona" uses "como" for the comparison, with the article. English says "like a person" with a different word class.
"Al menos" means "at least". "En los días buenos" keeps the article and puts the adjective after the noun.
"Mudarse de ciudad" is reflexive and takes "de". As a subject Spanish uses the infinitive, where English uses the "-ing" form.
"Pasados los treinta" is an absolute participle construction: literally "the thirties having passed". The participle agrees with what follows.
"Una forma rara de empezar de cero" chains two prepositions with "de", each doing a different job. "Empezar de cero" is the fixed phrase for starting over.
"Uno" is the impersonal subject where English uses "you". "Llevarse" is reflexive here, "to take along with oneself".
"Los mismos" always keeps the article, exactly as English keeps "the same".
"Solo" as an adverb means "only" and needs no accent. The verb comes before the subject, which Spanish allows freely.
"Los dos primeros meses" puts the cardinal before the ordinal — the opposite of English "the first two months". This order is fixed.
"Estar convencido" uses "estar", because it is a state. The imperfect describes how things were over that period.
"De que" is compulsory after "convencido". "Me había equivocado" is the pluperfect of a reflexive verb, with the pronoun before the auxiliary.
"Luego" means "then, afterwards". "Un camarero" has the indefinite article because he appears for the first time.
"Empezar a" keeps its compulsory "a", and "acordarse de" its compulsory "de" — two prepositions in a row, each belonging to a different verb.
"Colocarse" is reflexive: something settled by itself. "En silencio" means "quietly", and Spanish uses a noun phrase where English uses an adverb.
"Resulta que" again, the impersonal frame from the second phrase.
"Sentirse de un sitio" is an infinitive acting as subject. "Sentirse de" with a place is idiomatic and hard to translate literally.
"Sobre todo" means "mostly". "Repetición" needs no article here because it is a bare predicate.
"Echar de menos" is a three-word idiom that cannot be broken up. "Todavía" means "still".

"El piso antiguo" puts the adjective after the noun, where it means "old". Before it, "el antiguo piso", it would mean "my former flat" — and here both readings almost work, which is why the position matters.
"Por la luz" uses "por" for the cause, not "para". Confusing the two is the classic mistake.
"Pedir" takes an indirect object, so the pronoun is "le". The person is not named again because the previous context makes it clear.
"Un formulario sencillo" places the adjective after the noun. "Sencillo" means "simple, uncomplicated", while "simple" can suggest "simple-minded".
"A ser posible" is a fixed phrase, "if possible". "Para el jueves" uses "para" for a deadline; "por el jueves" would mean "around Thursday".
"Lo que llegó" is a subject clause with the neuter "lo", and the verb agrees in the singular.
"Tres semanas después" needs no preposition, and "después" follows the period.
The imperfect "era" for a description. "Pequeño y precioso" places both adjectives before the noun, which in Spanish makes them evaluative rather than classifying.
"Contemplar" here means "to cover, to provide for" — a formal use quite different from "to look at".
"Todos los casos" keeps the article after "todos", which is compulsory.
"Que nunca habíamos mencionado" uses the pluperfect and puts "nunca" before the verb, where it needs no extra "no".
"Para ser del todo justos" is a fixed parenthetical phrase, and "del todo" means "entirely".
"El código" keeps the article, as any subject noun does.
"Ser" for a lasting quality. "Realmente" means "genuinely".
"Y es también" places "también" after the verb.
"Lo único" uses the neuter article with an adjective, "the only thing". This is one of the constructions English has no direct equivalent for.
"Nadie más" puts "más" after the negative pronoun. "Saber" plus an infinitive means "to know how to", where English would use "can".
"Ahí hay" combines the adverb with the impersonal "hay", which never changes form.
"Yo mismo" adds the pronoun for emphasis and agrees in gender: a woman would say "yo misma".
"Seguir sin" plus the infinitive means "to still not have done something". It is a compact construction Spanish uses constantly and English lacks.
"Mi padre" uses a possessive instead of an article.
The present perfect "ha desarrollado" for something that has taken shape and still holds. In Spain this tense is the natural choice here.
"Una relación complicada con" places the adjective after the noun and takes "con". "Su tableta" uses the possessive, which is ambiguous between "his" and "her" in Spanish.
"Cada" is invariable and takes a singular noun.
"La vive como" uses the feminine object pronoun for "notificación", placed before the verb. "Vivir algo como" means "to experience it as".
"A su autoridad" takes "a" because "desafío" demands it. That government has to be learned with the noun.
"Ir a ver a alguien" chains two "a": one for the purpose and one for the person. The pronoun attaches to the infinitive.
"Pasar" plus a period means "to spend time". The subject is left unsaid.
The gerund "resolviendo" expresses what the time is spent on. "Conseguir" plus the infinitive means "to manage to", and the relative "que" cannot be dropped.
"El mes pasado" keeps the article and takes no preposition.
"Mandar" takes an indirect object, "me". "Un audio" is the everyday word for a voice message.
"Que eran" puts the verb in the plural, agreeing with "cuatro segundos" rather than with "audio". Spanish agrees with the predicate here, which surprises English speakers.
"Dejar de" plus the infinitive means "to stop doing". The "de" is compulsory.
The auxiliary is repeated: "he dejado ... y he empezado". Spanish repeats it more readily than English does.
"Empezar a" keeps its "a", and "simplemente" slips in between the auxiliary and the preposition without breaking anything.
"Él está más contento" uses "estar" for a state and adds the pronoun for contrast. Without "él" the sentence would still be correct but flatter.
"Tardar menos" means "to take less time". The parallel structure with the previous element is deliberate.
"Ninguno" takes a singular verb. "Nada" after it needs no extra "no", because the negation is already before the verb.
"El taller" keeps the article. The word means both "workshop" as an event and "workshop" as a repair shop.
"Se vendió como" is the impersonal "se", literally "it sold itself as". English says "was billed as", using a passive.
"Una sesión de alineación estratégica" chains the nouns with "de" and puts the adjective last. The order is exactly the reverse of English.
"En la práctica" keeps the article, as in the first phrase.
"Fueron once personas" puts the verb in the plural, agreeing with the people. English would use the singular "it was".
"Ponerse de acuerdo en" is a four-part idiom, and every piece is needed. The gerund "poniéndose" carries the reflexive pronoun attached to the end.
"Alguien" is invariable and always singular.
"La palabra" keeps its article because the word is named immediately after. Spanish uses angle quotes.
"De verdad" after the noun means "an actual one, a real one". Before the noun it would not work at all.
"Me gustaría decir" is the polite conditional of "gustar", which works backwards: the infinitive is the subject.
"Que protesté" needs its "que". The preterite marks a single act.
"Estuve mirando" is the preterite of "estar" plus a gerund, describing a completed stretch of time. The imperfect "estaba mirando" would leave it open-ended.
"Salir" without a complement means "to leave". The preterite for a finished action.
"Puntos de acción" links the nouns with "de".
"Dos de ellos" uses "de ellos" where a relative clause would be heavier. "Con responsable" needs no article: the noun is indefinite and singular by convention here.
"Para el viernes" uses "para" for a deadline, as in the fourth phrase.
"Todo aquello" uses the far demonstrative, which puts distance between the speaker and the events.
The pluperfect "se había evaporado", with the reflexive marking that it vanished by itself. "Sin ruido" is a noun phrase where English uses the adverb "quietly".
"Pasar por" means "to go through". The preterite places it as a finished period.
"Una época" has the indefinite article because it is mentioned for the first time.
"En la que" places the preposition before the relative, which is compulsory in careful Spanish. "Tomarse algo en serio" is reflexive and idiomatic.
"Había" is the imperfect of the impersonal "haber" and never agrees with what follows: never "habían".
"En la nevera" keeps the article. In Latin America the word would be "el refrigerador".
"Con nombre y horario" drops the articles because the nouns are indefinite and paired. Adding them would change the rhythm and the sense.
"Durante unas seis semanas" uses "durante" for the duration and "unas" for the approximation — the feminine plural of "uno" doing the work of English "about".
"Mi cocina" uses a possessive instead of an article.
"Oler" is stem-changing and adds an "h": "huelo", "hueles", "huele". "De maravilla" is a fixed phrase, "wonderfully".
"Llegar el trabajo" puts the verb before the subject, which Spanish uses to introduce something new.
"La masa madre" keeps the article, and both words together are the fixed term for a sourdough starter.
"Tener un final" is the collocation, not "hacer". "Discreto" placed after the noun keeps its plain meaning.
"Decir a la gente" needs the redundant pronoun "le" as well: Spanish doubles the indirect object even when it is named. "La gente" takes a singular verb.
"Volver a algo" takes "a", and "ello" is the neuter pronoun for a whole idea — rather formal, and mostly written.
"Cuando" plus the subjunctive "se calmen" because it points to the future. This is the rule English marks with nothing at all, and it is the single most useful subjunctive to get right.
"Los dos" means "both of us" and keeps the article.
"Que las cosas" opens the subordinate clause, and the article is compulsory in a general statement.
"No se calman" uses the indicative, because now it is a statement of fact rather than a projection. The contrast with the subjunctive two elements earlier is the whole point of the joke.
"Conocerse" is reciprocal: "we know each other". The pronoun comes before the verb.
"Desde hace tanto" uses "desde hace" for a stretch of time up to now, with the verb in the present. English needs a perfect tense here.
"Tanto ... que" is a two-part frame of consequence. "Saltarse" is reflexive and means "to skip".
"Llamar" with no subject pronoun: the ending is enough, and Spanish only adds the pronoun for contrast.
"Cada varios meses" is colloquial and means "every few months". "Cada" stays invariable.
"Mientras conduce" uses a full clause with the verb, where English can drop the subject and say "while driving".
"Nada importante" places the adjective after the pronoun, and "importante" has one form for both genders.
"Se dice" is the impersonal "se", equivalent to the English passive "is said".
"Los primeros diez minutos" puts the ordinal before the cardinal here, the reverse of the third phrase — because "primeros" is doing a different job in each.
"Cerca del final" contracts "de" and "el".
"Escapársele a alguien" again, as in the second phrase: "se le escapa" has both pronouns, and neither can be dropped.
"Una cosa de verdad" places "de verdad" after the noun, meaning "a real one".
"Ninguno de los dos" takes a singular verb, even though it refers to two people.
"Lo comenta" uses the neuter "lo" for the whole thing, placed before the verb. Spanish needs no preposition after "comentar".
"Consistir en" always takes "en". "Todo el acuerdo" keeps the article after "todo".
"Costarle a alguien" works backwards, like "gustar": the difficulty is the subject and the person is the indirect object. The conditional makes it hypothetical.
The infinitive is the subject of "costaría". "Esa amistad" uses the demonstrative instead of the article.
"A alguien" keeps the personal "a". "Menor de treinta" uses "de" after the comparative, not "que" — a genuine trap, since "que" is right in other comparisons.
"El chatbot" keeps the article. The word is a recent borrowing and is masculine.
"Tener ganas de" is the fixed way to say "to be keen", and it uses a noun where English uses an adjective. "Hoy" slips between the verb and the noun.
"De ayudarme" carries the "de" demanded by "ganas", with the pronoun attached to the infinitive.
"Preguntar" takes an indirect object, hence "me". The preterite for a single act.
"Si" here introduces an indirect yes-or-no question, not a condition, and carries no accent. "Había probado" is the pluperfect.
"Probar a" plus the infinitive means "to try doing". Spanish says "apagar y encender", in the reverse order from English "off and on".
"Lo había hecho" uses the neuter "lo" for the whole action, with the pluperfect. English can answer with the auxiliary alone; Spanish repeats the verb.
"Dos veces" is how Spanish says "twice"; there is no single word for it.
"Como ya le había explicado" uses "como" for "as". "Por escrito" is a fixed phrase with no article.
"A los once minutos" uses "a" plus the article for the moment when a period elapses. English would say "after eleven minutes".
"Ofrecerse a" is reflexive and takes "a". Without the pronoun the verb would mean "to offer something to somebody".
"Pasar a alguien con alguien" is the telephone idiom for putting someone through. The pronoun attaches to the infinitive.
"La persona" keeps the article and is grammatically feminine whatever the person's gender.
"La misma pregunta" keeps the article, and "hacer una pregunta" is the collocation — "preguntar una pregunta" would be wrong.
"Sonar" is a linking verb here, so an adjective follows: "avergonzada", agreeing in the feminine with "la persona" regardless of who it was.
"Un progreso" takes the indefinite article, where English "progress" is uncountable and takes none. This is a real difference in how the word behaves.
"En cierto modo" is a fixed phrase, "in a way". "Cierto" before the noun means "some, a certain".
"Ya" here means "now, at last". "Funcionar" is the verb for devices working.
"Dejar un trabajo" means to leave a job. The adjective follows the noun: "trabajo estable".
"Por algo" uses "por" for an exchange: one thing given up for another.
"Bastante menos seguro" stacks two degree words. "Bastante" here means "considerably", not "enough".
"Todo el mundo" means "everyone" and takes a singular verb, despite the plural sense.
"Que era valiente" needs its "que". The imperfect describes the situation as it was seen.
"Lo que se dice" combines the neuter "lo que" with the impersonal "se". Two impersonal constructions in a row are perfectly normal in Spanish.
"El primer año" uses the shortened "primer" before a masculine noun.
"Fue realmente duro" uses the preterite of "ser" for a closed period.
"A la ligera" is a fixed phrase, "lightly". "Lo" stands for the whole idea.
"Pero dejé" marks the turn, and the preterite closes the action.
"Dejar de" keeps its compulsory "de". "El reloj" keeps the article.
"A las cuatro de la tarde" uses "a las" for the hour and "de la tarde" for the part of the day. Both are needed, and "en la tarde" is not standard in Spain.
"Escrito así" is a participle used as a modifier, "written down like that". It agrees with the implied thing being written.
"Sonar a" plus a noun means "to sound like". "Poco" here is a noun, "not much".
"No lo es" uses the neuter "lo" to stand for the adjective already mentioned. Spanish cannot leave the verb bare the way English says "and it isn't".
The imperative with the pronoun attached to the end: "pregúntame". The written accent appears because the word grew longer.
"Dentro de cinco años" is the fixed way to say "in five years' time". "En cinco años" would suggest "within a span of five years".
"Quizá" with the subjunctive "tenga" expresses real uncertainty. With the indicative it would sound like a prediction, and the whole point of the ending is that it is not one.
